questions.question: Do not smoke within ____ of a vehicle carrying Class 3 or Division 2.1 materials.
questions.explanation: Do not smoke within 25 feet of a vehicle with hazardous materials. Class 3 includes flammable liquids. Division 2.1 includes flammable gases. Do not smoke or carry a lit cigarette, cigar, or pipe near these vehicles.

questions.question: You need a CDL with a hazmat endorsement to transport hazardous materials in:

options.text: A vehicle requiring a Class A license.
A vehicle requiring a Class B license.
A vehicle requiring a Class C license.

questions.explanation: You must have a CDL with a hazmat endorsement to drive any vehicle carrying hazardous materials, no matter what size.

questions.question: ____ warn others about hazardous materials.
questions.explanation: Placards are diamond-shaped signs placed on vehicles to warn others about hazardous materials. The shipper must place them correctly. The driver must check that the right placards are displayed.

questions.question: ____ is responsible for properly labeling hazardous materials.
questions.explanation: The shipper is responsible for packaging, marking, and labeling hazardous materials correctly. Drivers should verify that materials are labeled properly.

questions.question: If your vehicle breaks down while carrying explosives, you can warn other drivers using:

options.text: Standing on the roadway and waving your arms.
Keeping the driver's side door open.

questions.explanation: Use electric lights or reflective triangles to warn other drivers if your vehicle breaks down. Do not use flares near explosives or flammable materials because they could start a fire.

questions.question: When loading or unloading explosives, you should:

options.text: Use sharp-pointed tools to open the packages.

questions.explanation: Always turn off your engine before loading or unloading explosives. Never drop, throw, or roll packages containing explosives.

questions.question: A "Poison Inhalation Hazard" placard must be used when transporting:

options.text: More than 100 pounds of the product.
More than 50 pounds of the product.
The product in a leaking container.

questions.explanation: The "Poison Inhalation Hazard" placard must be displayed for any amount of materials that require it, along with the correct hazard class placard.

questions.question: On a shipping paper that lists both hazardous and non-hazardous materials, you can tell them apart by:

options.text: The hazardous materials being listed first.
The non-hazardous materials being written in pencil.
The hazardous materials being listed in red ink.
The hazardous materials being written larger than the non-hazardous materials.

questions.correctAnswerText: The hazardous materials being listed first.
questions.explanation: Hazardous materials must be distinguished on shipping papers in one of three ways: listed first, highlighted in a contrasting color, or marked with an "X" in a column titled "HM."

questions.question: If "Inhalation Hazard" appears on a shipping paper, what placard should the shipper provide?

options.text: Poison Gas or Poison Inhalation Hazard

questions.correctAnswerText: Poison Gas or Poison Inhalation Hazard
questions.explanation: If "Inhalation Hazard" is on the shipping paper or package, display the "Poison Inhalation Hazard" or "Poison Gas" placard, whichever is appropriate.

questions.question: Shipping papers:

options.text: Are not needed for most shipments.
Should be stored in a special compartment in the cab.
Can be kept as a digital file.

questions.explanation: Shipping papers are required for all hazardous materials shipments. They inform drivers and dock workers about the cargo and its hazards.

questions.question: If "Inhalation Hazard" appears on shipping papers, what must you do?

options.text: Use an inhalation hazard placard only if you are carrying more than 100 pounds.
Use an inhalation hazard placard for any amount of the material.
Provide air masks to anyone handling the cargo.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use an inhalation hazard placard for any amount of the material.
questions.explanation: If "Inhalation Hazard" appears on a package or shipping paper, you must display the proper inhalation hazard placard and any other required placards. This applies no matter how much material you are carrying.

questions.question: Where can a person attend a placarded vehicle?

options.text: Either awake or asleep inside the vehicle.

questions.explanation: A person attending a placarded vehicle must be awake inside the vehicle or within 100 feet of it. If they are outside the vehicle, they must have a clear view of it. They cannot be in the sleeper berth.

questions.question: What is a sign that your shipment may contain hazardous materials?

options.text: The shipper works in a business that typically uses hazardous materials, such as fireworks or pest control.
Your last shipment was labeled as hazardous.
The shipper's business is in a bad area of town.

questions.correctAnswerText: The shipper works in a business that typically uses hazardous materials, such as fireworks or pest control.
questions.explanation: One sign that a shipment contains hazardous materials is that the shipper is in a business that normally deals with such materials. Examples include paint dealers, chemical suppliers, and pest control companies.

questions.question: When can you move a vehicle that does not have proper placards?

options.text: To make room for other vehicles.
If the vehicle will travel less than 10 miles.

questions.explanation: A vehicle must have proper placards before it can be driven. An improperly placarded vehicle can only be moved if it is necessary to protect lives or property in an emergency.

questions.question: What does a driver need to accept a package (unless it is clearly unsafe)?
questions.explanation: When a shipper packages hazardous materials, they certify that the package meets Hazardous Materials Regulations. You may accept this certification unless the package is clearly unsafe or does not meet regulations.

questions.question: What must you do when crossing railroad tracks while transporting chlorine?

options.text: Reduce your speed before crossing the tracks.
You can proceed if no warning lights are flashing.
You can proceed if no other vehicles are visible.

questions.explanation: When transporting any amount of chlorine, you must always stop at a railroad crossing 15 to 50 feet from the nearest track.

questions.question: What should you do with the engine before loading or unloading flammable liquids?
questions.explanation: You should turn off the engine before loading or unloading flammable liquids. The only exception is if you need to run the engine to operate a pump.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT considered a hazardous material?
questions.explanation: Hazardous materials are products that pose risks to health, safety, and property during transportation. These include explosives, flammable and poisonous gases, and flammable and other hazardous solids. Regular rocks are not hazardous materials.

questions.question: Which agency helps coordinate emergency response to chemical hazards?

options.text: The United Center for Chemical Assistance

questions.explanation: The National Response Center helps police and firefighters coordinate emergency response to chemical hazards.

questions.question: Who is responsible for putting placards on a vehicle?
questions.explanation: The shipper provides the placards, but the driver is responsible for actually placing them on the vehicle.

questions.question: If you notice a cargo leak, how should you identify the leaking hazardous materials?
questions.explanation: If cargo is leaking, check the shipping papers, labels, or package location to identify the materials. Do not touch or smell the leaking materials. This could cause injury or death.

questions.question: If hazardous materials are leaking and the driver has no phone, what should they do?

options.text: Drive to find a phone to alert emergency personnel.
Drive to a hazardous materials cleanup facility.
Send someone else to get help.

questions.correctAnswerText: Send someone else to get help.
questions.explanation: If hazardous materials leak, do not move the vehicle more than necessary. Driving spreads contamination. Instead, park the vehicle, secure it, stay with it, and call for help. If you have no phone, send someone else to get help.

questions.question: If an explosives package is oily or damp, what should the driver do?

options.text: Use towels to absorb the liquid.

questions.explanation: Never transport damaged explosives packages. Do not accept any package that is damp or has an oily stain.

questions.question: When transporting Division 1.3 materials, what should the floor liner be made of?
questions.explanation: Use a floor liner when transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 materials. The floor must be tight and the liner must be non-metallic or non-ferrous metal. Non-ferrous metals contain no iron.

questions.question: If you suspect a leak in radioactive material cargo, what should you do?

options.text: Go to the local fire department.
Pick up any loose pieces of radioactive material.
Continue carrying the cargo, but avoid touching affected areas.
Do not drive the vehicle until it has been cleaned.

questions.correctAnswerText: Do not drive the vehicle until it has been cleaned.
questions.explanation: If you suspect a leak or broken package in radioactive material, tell your dispatcher or supervisor right away. Do not touch or breathe in the material. Do not use the vehicle until it has been cleaned or checked with a survey meter.

questions.question: What does a material's hazard class show?

options.text: How fast the material must reach its destination
What country the material came from

questions.explanation: Hazardous materials are divided into nine hazard classes. The hazard class tells you what risks the material poses.

questions.question: If a package says "Inhalation Hazard," which placard must be used?
questions.explanation: If "Inhalation Hazard" is on a package or shipping paper, use the "Poison Inhalation Hazard" or "Poison Gas" placard.

questions.question: What hazard class are explosive materials?
questions.explanation: Class 1 materials are items that can explode or catch fire.

questions.question: What is a Class 7 hazardous material?
questions.explanation: Class 7 materials are radioactive.

questions.question: Which agency does a background check when you apply for a HazMat endorsement?
questions.explanation: To get a hazardous materials endorsement, you must pass a background check from the Transportation Security Administration (TSA).
